newsitem.title: Belgium: Parliament agrees Belgian child sex scandal report.
newsitem.headline: Parliament agrees Belgian child sex scandal report.

text.p: The Belgian parliament put aside some clear differences of opinion on Friday to approve unanimously a scathing report on bungled investigations into the country's child rape and murder scandals.
"We are setting ourselves an ambitious goal," Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene told the packed lower house before the vote.
"Respect for victims, modernisation of the justice system, and reform of the police so that the dramas we have witnessed are never repeated," he added.
"That is an undertaking of the government and my personal undertaking to the parents," Dehaene said.
The vote by the 137 deputies followed two days of debate that exposed tensions between the Francophone Liberal opposition party and the four parties in the centre-left coalition.

But in the end, and in the knowledge that public opinion would slaughter them if they let party politics stand in the way of the report by the special parliamentary commission, they buried their differences and voted together.

The report, which follows six months of often televised hearings that riveted the nation, spares no one in its description of the shambolic investigations into child kidnappings, rapes and murders that came to light last August.
The bodies of five young girls have been found, and police are still looking for more. Two convicted child rapists -- Marc Dutroux and Patrick Derochette -- have been charged with murder.
The all-party report makes recommendations ranging from creation of a single police force -- replacing three rival forces -- to reform of the whole justice system.

It says that some at least of the dead girls might have been rescued alive had police and magistrates spent more time investigating than fighting among each other, but suggests that sheer incompetence might not have been the only factor.
The commission has been given until the end of September to study whether Dutroux and Derochette and their accomplices might have escaped arrest earlier because of high-level protection.
In October more than 250,000 people marched through Brussels to show support for the victims and demonstrate their disgust at a system seen as at best incompetent and at worse as corrupt.
"We must reestablish confidence in our institutions," Dehaene said. "The recommendations of the commission set out a clear work programme for the government."
Proof that public faith in the Belgian government and legal systems is at rock bottom was provided on Friday by an opinion poll in Le Vif L'Express weekly magazine.
The poll of 1,000 Belgians showed that 37 percent had no confidence at all in the government, 36 percent had no faith in the justice system and 29 percent had no faith in the gendarmerie.

Dehaene noted that several of the proposed reforms were already in the pipeline. The rules on the early release from prison of sex offenders were being changed, and amendments were in progress ending the political promotion of magistrates.

But it was reform of the police that split the deputies, with some -- notably Dutch speakers -- calling for a unified national police force and others -- notably the Francophone Liberals -- arguing strongly against it.
The Liberals also called for Interior Minister Johan Vande Lanotte and Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck to resign.

Ecologist Party deputy Vincent Decroly summed up the general tone when on Thursday he put Dehaene on notice that his party would call for the government's resignation unless there was clear evidence of reform progress within three months.
